senses: advice, counsel (when offered by someone with credibility and strong influence)
warrant, authenticity (something that provides assurance or confirmation)
power conferred, will, decree, order, rights, command (often refers to the will or decree of the senate)
la:noun:auctoritas.html:
auctōrĭtas (not autōr- nor authōr-), ātis, f.
auctor
, acc. to the different signiff. of that word,
In gen., a producing, production, invention, cause (very rare; syn.: auctoramentum, sententia, judicium, consilium, vis, pondus, favor, gratia): quod si exquiratur usque ab stirpe auctoritas (sc. rumoris),originator, inventor,: ejus facti qui sint principes et inventores, qui denique auctoritatis ejus et inventionis comprobatores,: utrum poëtae Stoicos depravārint, an Stoici poëtis dederint auctoritatem, non facile dixerim,.—
Esp.,
A view, opinion, judgment: errat vehementer, si quis in orationibus nostris auctoritates nostras consignatas se habere arbitratur,: reliquum est, ut de Q. Catuli auctoritate et sententiā dicendum esse videatur,; : Mihi quidem ex animo eximi non potest, esse deos, id tamen ipsum, quod mihi persuasum est auctoritate majorum, cur ita sit, nihil tu me doces,: plus apud me antiquorum auctoritas valet,.—
Counsel, advice, persuasion, encouragement to something (esp. if made with energy and sustained by the authority and influence of the counsellor; cf. auctor, I. C.): auctoritatem defugere,: Jubeo, cogo atque impero. Numquam defugiam auctoritatem, Ruhnk.: attende jam, Torquate, quam ego defugiam auctoritatem consulatūs mei, how little pleased (ironically) I am that the occurrences of my consulship are ascribed to my exertions, my influence, : cujus (Reguli) cum valuisset auctoritas, captivi retenti sunt,: jure, legibus, auctoritate omnium, qui consulebantur, testamentum fecerat,: ejus (Sexti) mihi vivit auctoritas,: his rebus adducti et auctoritate Orgetorigis permoti etc.,: ut per auctoritatem earum civitatium suae preces nuper repudiatae faciliorem aditum ad senatum haberent, i. e. agentibus, intervenientibus, —Also consolatory exhortation, consolation, comfort: his autem litteris animum tuum...amicissimi hominis auctoritate confirmandum etiam atque etiam puto,.—
Will, pleasure, decision, bidding, command, precept, decree: si ad verba rem deflectere velimus, consilium autem eorum, qui scripserunt, et rationem et auctoritatem relinquamus?: verba servire hominum consiliis et auctoritatibus,: legio auctoritatem Caesaris persecuta est,: nisi legiones ad Caesaris auctoritatem se contulissent,under his command, guidance,—Hence,
Esp., in political lang., t. t.
Senatūs auctoritas,
The will of the senate: agrum Picenum contra senatūs auctoritatem dividere,.—More freq.,
A decree of the senate, = Senatūs consultum: Senatūs vetus auctoritas de Bacchanalibus,: sine senatūs auctoritate foedus facere,: Senatūs auctoritas gravissima intercessit,: responditque ita ex auctoritate senatūs consul,: imperio non populi jussu, non ex auctoritate patrum dato,: Neminem exulum nisi ex Senatūs auctoritate restituit,: citra senatūs populique auctoritatem, —Hence the superscription to the decrees of the Senate: SENATVS. CONSVLTI. AVCTORITAS., abbrev., S. C. A.,.—Sometimes between senatūs auctoritas and senatūs consultum this distinction is to be made, that the former designates a decision of the senate, invalidated by the protestation of the tribune of the people or by the people themselves; the latter, one that is passed without opposition,; .—
Auctoritas populi, the popular will or decision: isti principes et sibi et ceteris populi universi auctoritati parendum esse fateantur,; so, publica,; .—
Auctoritas collegii (pontificum), ; cf. and 21.—
Liberty, ability, power, authority to do according to one's pleasure: qui habet imperium a populo Romano auctoritatem legum dandarum ab senatu,: Verres tantum sibi auctoritatis in re publicā suscepit, ut, etc.,: Invita in hoc loco versatur oratio; videtur enim auctoritatem adferre peccandi,: Senatūs faciem secum attulerat auctoritatemque populi Romani,.—
Might, power, authority, reputation, dignity, influence, weight (very freq.): ut vostra auctoritas Meae auctoritati fautrix adjutrixque sit, prol. alt. 40: aequitate causae et auctoritate suā aliquem commovere,: id maximā auctoritate philosophi adfirmant,: Digna est memoriā Q. Catuli cum auctoritas tum verecundia,: optimatium auctoritatem deminuere,; so, auctoritatem habere,; : adripere,; : facere,to procure, obtain,: Grandis auctoritatis es et bene regis regnum Israël, * : imminuere,: levare,: fructus capere auctoritatis,: Quae sunt voluptates corporis cum auctoritatis praemiis comparandae? et saep. —Transf. to things, importance, significance, weight, power, worth, value, estimation: bos in pecuariā maximā debet esse auctoritate,: sunt certa legum verba... quo plus auctoritatis habeant, paulo antiquiora,more weight, force,: totius hujusce rei quae sit vis, quae auctoritas, quod pondus, ignorant,: utilitatis species falsa ab honestatis auctoritate superata est,: cum antea per aetatem nondum hujus auctoritatem loci attingere auderem, of this honorable place, i. e. the rostra, : bibliothecas omnium philosophorum mihi videtur XII. tabularum libellus auctoritatis pondere superare,; ; Dolab. ap. : auctoritas praecipua lupo (pisci),: Post eum (Maecenatum) interiit auctoritas sapori (pullorum

asinorum), Jan: unguentorum,: auctoritas dignitasque formae,.—Also of feigned, assumed authority: nec cognovi quemquam, qui majore auctoritate nihil diceret,that said nothing with a greater air of authority,.—

An example, pattern, model: omnium superiorum auctoritatem repudiare,: memoriā digna juventuti rei publicae capessendae auctoritas disciplinaque,: valuit auctoritas,; so ; : tu is es qui in disputando non tuum judicium sequare, sed auctoritati aliorum pareas,; —
A warrant, security for establishing a fact, assertion, etc., credibility: cum ea (justitia) sine prudentiā satis habeat auctoritatis,: desinant putare, auctoritatem esse in eo testimonio, cujus auctor inventus est nemo,: Quid vero habet auctoritatis furor iste, quem divinum vocatis?: tollitur omnis auctoritas somniorum,: cum ad vanitatem accessit auctoritas,.—
Meton., the things which serve for the verification or establishment of a fact.
A record, document: videt legationes, cum publicis auctoritatibus convenisse,: nihil putas valere in judiciis civitatum auctoritates ac litteras,, § 146.—
The name of a person who is security for something, authority: cum auctoritates principum conjurationis colligeret,: sed tu auctoritates contemnis, ratione pugnas,.—Hence for the names of persons present at the drawing up of a decree of the senate: quod in auctoritatibus praescriptis exstat,: Senatūs consultum, quod tibi misi, factum est auctoritatesque perscriptae, Cael. ap. .—
Right of possession (cf. auctor, II. F. 1.): lex usum et auctoritatem fundi jubet esse biennium,: usūs auctoritas fundi biennium est,; so ; ; Lex Atin. ap. ; cf. Hugo, Rechtsgesch. p. 217 sq.—So in the laws of the XII. Tables: ADVERSVS. HOSTEM. AETERNA. AVCTORITAS., against a stranger the right of possession is perpetual (i. e. a stranger cannot, by prescription, obtain the right of possession to the property of a Roman), ap. .—
In jurid. lang., a guaranty, security, .

senses: one who gives increase (hence: an originator, causer, doer, founder)
la:noun:auctor.html:
auctor (incorrectly written autor or author), ōris, comm.
id.
,
he that brings about the existence of any object, or promotes the increase or prosperity of it, whether he first originates it, or by his efforts gives greater permanence or continuance to it; to be differently translated according to the object, creator, maker, author, inventor, producer, father, founder, teacher, composer, cause, voucher, supporter, leader, head, etc. (syn.: conditor, origo, consiliarius, lator, suasor, princeps, dux).
Lit.
Of persons, a progenitor, father, ancestor: L. Brutus, praeclarus auctor nobilitatis tuae,the founder, progenitor of your nobility,: generis,; so , and : tu sanguinis ultimus auctor,; so , and 13, 142: tantae propaginis,: originis,: gentis,: auctores parentes animarum,: auctore ab illo ducit originem,: Sive neglectum genus et nepotes Respicis auctor,: mihi Tantalus auctor,: auctores saxa fretumque tui,: Juppiter e terrā genitam mentitur, ut auctor Desinat inquiri,.—Of animals, .—
Of buildings, etc., founder, builder: Trojae Cynthius auctor,: murorum Romulus auctor, (augur, Müll.): auctor posuisset in oris Moenia,: porticus auctoris Livia nomen habet,: amphitheatri,: omnia sub titulo tantum suo ac sine ullā pristini auctoris memoriā,.—
Of works of art, a maker, artist: statua auctoris incerti,: apparuit summam artis securitatem auctori placaisse, id. praef. § 27.—
Transf.
In gen., the originator, executor, performer, doer, cause, occasion of other things (freq. interchanged with actor): tametsi haud quaquam par gloriá sequitur scriptorem et auctorem rerum, tamen etc., Kritz (cf. without rerum: Suam quisque culpam auctores ad negotia transferunt, id. J. 1, 4): praeclari facinoris,: facti,; : cum perquirerent auctorem facti,: optimi statūs auctor,: honoris,: vitae,: salutis,: fidei,: funeris,: necis,; 9, 214: mortis,: vulneris,; 8, 418: plagae,: seditionis sectae,.—Also, in gen., one from whom any thing proceeds or comes: auctor in incerto est: jaculum de parte sinistrā Venit,i. e. the sender,; so, teli,: muneris,the giver,; 5, 657, 7, 157 al.: meritorum, al.—
An author of scientific or literary productions.
An investigator: non sordidus auctor Naturae verique,.—And as imparting learning, a teacher: quamquam in antiquissimā philosophiā Cratippo auctore versaris,: dicendi gravissimus auctor et magister Plato,: divini humanique juris auctor celeberrimus,: Servius Sulpicius, juris civilis auctor,; ; .—
The author of a writing, a writer: ii quos nunc lectito auctores,: ingeniosus poëta et auctor valde bonus,: scripta auctori perniciosa suo,: Belli Alexandrini Africique et Hispaniensis incertus auctor est,; : sine auctore notissimi versus,i. e. anonymous verses,; so ; —Meton. of cause for effect, for a literary production, writing, work: in evolvendis utriusque linguae auctoribus, etc.,. —In partic., the author of historical works, an historian (with and without rerum): ego cautius posthac historiam attingam, te audiente, quem rerum Romanarum auctorem laudare possum religiosissimum,; so, Matrem Antoniam non apud auctores rerum, non diurnā actorum scripturā reperio ullo insigni officio functam,; (diff. from auctor rerum in II. A.): Polybius bonus auctor in primis,; so ; ; ; —With historiae (eccl. Lat.): historiae congruit auctori,.—Hence, in gen., one that gives an account of something, a narrator, reporter, informant (orally or in writing): sibi insidias fieri: se id certis auctoribus comperisse,: celeberrimos auctores habeo tantam victoribus irreverentiam fuisse, ut, etc.,: criminis ficti auctor, i. e. nuntius,: Non haec tibi nuntiat auctor Ambiguus,; 12, 58; 12, 61; 12, 532.—Hence, auctorem esse, with acc. and inf., to relate, recount: Auctores sunt ter novenis punctis interfici hominem,: Fabius Rustiçus auctor est scriptos esse ad Caecinam Tuscum codicillos,: Auctor est Julius Marathus ante paucos quam nasceretur menses prodigium Romae factum (esse) publice, etc., et saep.—
One by whose influence, advice, command, etc., any thing is done, the cause, occasion, contriver, instigator, counsellor, adviser, promoter; constr. sometimes with ut, acc. and inf., or gen. gerund.: quid mihi es auctor (what do you counsel me?) huic ut mittam? ; ; : idne estis auctores mihi?: mihique ut absim, vehementer auctor est,: Gellium ipsis (philosophis) magno opere auctorem fuisse, ut controversiarum facerent modum,: ut propinqui de communi sententiā coërcerent, auctor fuit,; ; : a me consilium petis, qui sim tibi auctor in Siciliāne subsidas, an proficiscare,: ego quidem tibi non sim auctor, si Pompeius Italiam reliquit, te quoque profugere, Att. ap. : ne auctor armorum duxque deesset, Auct. B. G. 8, 47: auctor facinori non deerat,: auctores Bibulo fuere tantundem pollicendi,: auctores restituendae tribuniciae potestatis,; so : auctor singulis universisque conspirandi simul et ut... communem causam juvarent,—So freq. in the abl. absol.: me, te, eo auctore, at my, your, his instance, by my

advice, command, etc.: non me quidem Faciet auctore, hodie ut illum decipiat,: an paenitebat flagiti, te auctore quod fecisset Adulescens?: quare omnes istos me auctore deridete atque contemnite,: quia calida fomenta non proderant, frigidis curari coactus auctore Antonio Musā,; ; ; : agis Carminibus grates et dis auctoribus horum, the promoters or authors of spells, .—

Esp., in political lang., t. t.
Auctor legis.
One who proposes a law, a mover, proposer (very rare): quarum legum auctor fuerat, earum suasorem se haud dubium ferebat,: Quid desperatius, qui ne ementiendo quidem potueris auctorem adumbrare meliorem,.—
One who advises the proposal of a law, and exerts all his influence to have it passed, a supporter (stronger than suasor; cf. : alium dicente, auctore eo Senatum se adīsse, verba mutare et pro auctore suasorem dicere coegit): isti rationi neque lator quisquam est inventus neque auctor umquam bonus,: cum ostenderem, si lex utilis plebi Romanae mihi videretur, auctorem me atque adjutorem futurum (esse),; : quo auctore societatem cum Perseo junxerunt,; ; —Sometimes in connection with suasor: atque hujus deditionis ipse Postumius suasor et auctor fuit,: Nisi quis retinet, idem suasor auctorque consilii ero,—
Of a senate which accepts or adopts a proposition for a law, a confirmer, ratifier: nunc cum loquar apud senatores populi Romani, legum et judiciorum et juris auctores,.—Poet., in gen., a law-giver: animum ad civilia vertet Jura suum, legesque feret justissimus auctor,; and of one who establishes conditions of peace: leges captis justissimus auctor imposuit,. —Hence, auctores fieri, to approve, accept, confirm a law: cum de plebe consulem non accipiebat, patres ante auctores fieri coëgerit,: Decreverunt ut, cum populus regem jussisset, id sic ratum esset, si patres auctores fierent,; ; ; 2, 56; 6, 42; 8, 12 al.—
Auctor consilii publici, he who has the chief voice in the senate, a leader: hunc rei publicae rectorem et consilii publici auctorem esse habendum,; . —Also absol.: regem Ariobarzanem, cujus salutem a senatu te auctore, commendatam habebam,by your influence, and the decree of the senate occasioned by it,; cf. Gron. ad .—
One who is an exemplar, a model, pattern, type of any thing: Caecilius, malus auctor Latinitatis,: nec litterarum Graecarum, nec philosophiae jam ullum auctorem requiro,; cf. Wopk. Lect. Tull. p. 34: unum cedo auctorem tui facti, unius profer exemplum,i. e. who has done a similar thing,: Cato omnium virtutum auctor,—
One that becomes security for something, a voucher, bail, surety, witness: id ita esse ut credas, rem tibi auctorem dabo,: auctorem rumorem habere,: fama nuntiabat te esse in Syriā; auctor erat nemo,: non si mihi Juppiter auctor Spondeat,: gravis quamvis magnae rei auctor,: auctorem levem, nec satis fidum super tantā re Patres rati,: urbs auspicato deis auctoribus in aeternum condita,under the guaranty of the gods,.—Also with acc. and inf.: auctores sumus tutam ibi majestatem Romani nominis fore,.—
In judic. lang., t. t.
A seller, vender (inasmuch as he warrants the right of possession of the thing to be sold, and transfers it to the purchaser; sometimes the jurists make a distinction between auctor primus and auctor secundus; the former is the seller himself, the latter the bail or security whom the former brings, ; cf. Salmas. Mod. Usur. pp. 728 and 733): quod a malo auctore emīssent,: auctor fundi,; : Inpero (auctor ego sum), ut tu me quoivis castrandum loces, Wagn.; ; , 12.—Trop.: auctor beneficii populi Romani,.—
A guardian, trustee (of women and minors): dos quam mulier nullo auctore dixisset,: majores nostri nullam ne privatam quidem rem agere feminas sine auctore voluerunt,: pupillus obligari tutori eo auctore non potest,.—
In espousals, auctores are the witnesses of the marriage contract (parents, brothers, guardians, relatives, etc.): nubit genero socrus, nullis auspicibus, nullis auctoribus,.—
An agent, factor, spokesman, intercessor, champion: praeclarus iste auctor suae civitatis,: (Plancius) princeps inter suos... maximarum societatum auctor, plurimarum magister,: meae salutis,: doloris sui, querelarum, etc.,!*? In class. Lat. auctor is also used as fem.: eas aves, quibus auctoribus etc.,: Et hostes aderant et (Theoxena) auctor mortis instabat,: auctor ego (Juno) audendi,; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. Paul. ex Müll. The distinction which the grammarians, , Prob. p. 1452 sq. P., and others make between auctor fem. and auctrix, that auctrix would refer more to the lit. signif. of the verb, augeo, while auctor fem. has more direct relation to the prevailing signif. of its noun, auctoritas, is unfounded.

la:verb:aucto.html:
aucto, āre,
v. freq. [augeo], to increase or enlarge much (perh. only in the foll. exs.): res rationesque vostrorum omnium Bono atque amplo auctare lucro,: Unde omnis natura creet res auctet alatque,: Salve, teque bonā Juppiter auctet ope,.

la:noun:auctio.html:
auctĭo, ōnis, f.
augeo
.
An increasing, increase, αὐξησις: auctio frumenti et tributorum,: dierum,: rerum crescentium, Paul. ex Müll.—
A sale by increase of bids, a public sale, auction. Auctions were held either in an open place, or in particular rooms or halls, called atria auctionaria (v. auctionarius), or simply atria (). There was a spear (hasta) set up therein, as the legal sign of the sale, like our red flag; the price was called out by a crier (praeco), and the article sold was adjudged to the highest bidder by the magistrate who was present. A money-broker (argentarius) was also present to note down the price and receive the money or security for it; v. Smith, Dict. Antiq. (this is the class. signif. of the word): auctionem facere,-94; so ; ; ; ; : Dicam auctionis causam, ut animo gaudeant, Ipse egomet quam ob rem auctionem praedicem,announce,; so, auctionis diem obire,: proscribere,; and proponere,: proferre,to defer, adjourn,: amplissima praedia ex auctionibus hastae minimo addixit, by the sales of the spear, i. e. by auctions (v. supra), (cf.: praebere caput dominā venale sub hastā,): auctio hereditaria constituta,: auctionis tabula, (v. auctionalis): auctio fortunae regiae,: vendere aliquid in auctione,by auction,: res in auctione venit,: ex auctione rem emere,: auctionem dimittere,. —
Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), goods to be sold by auction: cum auctionem venderet, (B. and K.; others, auctione).

la:verb:auctoro.gloss: to become security for, give a pledge as bondsman
senses: to become security for, give a pledge as bondsman
to bind or oblige oneself, hire oneself out
la:verb:auctoro.html:
auctōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (access. form auctōror, āri, ; ; ; ) [auctor].
To become security for, to give a pledge as bondsman, ; .—Trop., in the pass.: observatio satis auctorata consensūs patrocinio,confirmed, supported,.—
More freq. se auctorare, or pass. auctorari, to bind or oblige one's self to something, to hire one's self out for some service (mostly post-Aug.; never in Cic.): vindemitor auctoratus,.—Esp. of gladiators: Quid refert, uri virgis ferroque necari Auctoratus eas, * (qui se vendunt ludo (gladiatorio) auctorati vocantur; auctoratio enim dicitur venditio gladiatorum, Acro): proximo munere inter novos auctoratos ferulis vapulare placet,: auctoratus ob sepeliendum patrem,; .—Hence, in the pun: ipsum magis auctoratum populum Romanum circumferens,i. e. brought into greater danger than the gladiators,.—Hence,
In gen., to bind: eo pignore velut auctoratum sibi proditorem ratus est,; .— *
Sibi mortem aliquā re, to bring death to one's self by some means, .

senses: to chase, strive for; to be on the lookout, lie in wait or watch for
la:verb:aucupor.html:
aucŭpor, ātus, 1, v. dep. and
act. [auceps], to go bird-catching or fowling.
Lit.: Alio loco ut seras ac colas silvam caeduam, alio ubi aucupare,; .—Also of taking bees: spes aucupandi examina,.—
Trop., to chase, give chase to, strive for, be on the look-out for, lie in wait for; watch for, etc. (a favorite figure in prose and poetry; in Cic. perh. twenty times; syn.: insidior, sequor): Viden scelestus ut aucupatur?how he gives chase?: nos longis navibus tranquillitates aucupaturi eramus,: tempus,: alicujus imbecillitatem,: ut omni ex genere orationem aucuper, et omnis undique flosculos carpam atque delibem,; ; ; ; ; 19, 63; : L. Cassio omnes ramusculos popularis aurae aucupante,; : occasionem, Auct. B. Afr. 3 fin.: obtrectatione alienae scientiae famam sibi, praef. § 30; 33, 2, 8, § 32: studium populi ac favorem,: reconditas voces,: absentiam alicujus,: somnos,.!*?
Act. form aucŭpo, āre, to watch for, etc.: fructus verborum aures aucupant, Enn. ap. : prospectum aucupo, Pac. ib.: in consilio id reges Argivom aucupant, Att. ib.: id ego aucupavi, Titinn. ib.: Paulisper mane: Aucupemus ex insidiis clanculum quam rem gerant,: num quis est, Sermonem nostrum qui aucupet,; so : ex insidiis aucupa,: qui aucupet me quid agam,: Lepide, mecastor, aucupavi,.—*
Pass. form aucupor: Multa divulgata ac per rumorem vicissim aucupata discuntur,.

auctusfero

fruit-bearing, fruitful, fertile: terrae, Cic. ap. , 5, 8 (Orell. IV. 2, p. 515), as a free transl. of Hom. Od. 18, 135 and 136.

Lit.: corporis auctus,; : Hic natura suis refrenat viribus auctum,; ; : auxilium appellatum ab auctu, Müll.: vos (Divi Divaeque) bonis auctibus auxitis,; : aquarum,; : diei,.—Poet.: caedere arboris auctum, the abundance of a tree, for a large tree, ; so, nec lorica tenet distenti corporis auctum,.—

la:verb:auctionor.gloss: to hold an auction or public sale; make a sale by auction
senses: to hold an auction or public sale; make a sale by auction
la:verb:auctionor.html:
auctĭōnor, ātus, 1, v. dep.
id.

An increasing, increase, αὐξησις: auctio frumenti et tributorum,: dierum,: rerum crescentium, Paul. ex Müll.—
A sale by increase of bids, a public sale, auction. Auctions were held either in an open place, or in particular rooms or halls, called atria auctionaria (v. auctionarius), or simply atria (). There was a spear (hasta) set up therein, as the legal sign of the sale, like our red flag; the price was called out by a crier (praeco), and the article sold was adjudged to the highest bidder by the magistrate who was present. A money-broker (argentarius) was also present to note down the price and receive the money or security for it; v. Smith, Dict. Antiq. (this is the class. signif. of the word): auctionem facere,-94; so ; ; ; ; : Dicam auctionis causam, ut animo gaudeant, Ipse egomet quam ob rem auctionem praedicem,announce,; so, auctionis diem obire,: proscribere,; and proponere,: proferre,to defer, adjourn,: amplissima praedia ex auctionibus hastae minimo addixit, by the sales of the spear, i. e. by auctions (v. supra), (cf.: praebere caput dominā venale sub hastā,): auctio hereditaria constituta,: auctionis tabula, (v. auctionalis): auctio fortunae regiae,: vendere aliquid in auctione,by auction,: res in auctione venit,: ex auctione rem emere,: auctionem dimittere,. —
Meton. (abstr. pro concr.), goods to be sold by auction: cum auctionem venderet, (B. and K.; others, auctione).

That for which one binds himself to some service or duty (as that of soldiers, gladiators, etc.), wages, pay, hire, reward.
